mars.why: Mars has no rain; hyper-arid deserts keep ancient surfaces and salts like Mars.
Mars is bare rock and dust: no soil, no plants.
No life signal at the surface; low NDVI means rover tests see bare terrain.
Martian ground is dry; damp soil behaves nothing like regolith.
The Martian air is extremely dry.
Mars is cold (mean about −60 °C): freezing seasons test equipment.
Big temperature swings, like Mars' strong day/season contrast.
High ground has thinner air and more UV, a step towards Mars' 0.6 kPa.
Mars' surface is rock and dust with ice hidden below; a thick ice sheet is not Mars-like.

moon.why: The lunar south pole is brutally cold (−170 °C in shadow, −230 °C in permanently dark craters).
Polar sites get the Sun low on the horizon all year, the lighting Artemis crews will work in.
Water ice is the reason to go to the south pole; icy ground tests ice prospecting and drilling.
Rock and loose debris, no soil or plants, like regolith terrain.
Very dry polar deserts preserve frozen ground.
High, isolated terrain: thin air, strong UV, rough access.
Long dark winters and light summers, a proxy for polar day/night cycles.

moon.name: Lunar south pole
conditions: about −170 °C in shadow to +50 °C in sunlight; below −230 °C inside permanently shadowed craters
regolith: sharp, glassy dust and rock; water ice in shadowed craters
Sun skims the horizon; some ridges lit most of the year, crater floors never
no magnetic field or air: full cosmic rays and solar particles
sources: NASA Artemis III candidate landing regions

mars.name: Mars
conditions: mean about −60 °C; from about +20 °C at noon near the equator to −125 °C at the poles
basaltic dust and rock; perchlorate salts; water ice under the surface at high latitudes
no liquid water at the surface today; ancient river deltas such as Jezero
thin air and no global magnetic field: strong UV and cosmic rays
sources: Perchlorate found by Phoenix (Hecht et al., Science 2009)
